lens: clarity and depth for a curious 15-year-old and an expert at once (this film has no AlexNet/transformer sequences; the lens was applied to its three deep dives: ternary-to-ReLU, loops/state as fixed arithmetic, gradients through a program, plus ch02's history and ch05's compilation)
runtimeCheck: script.mjs assemble --check: 12 chapters, 101 shots, 183 lines, 2,427 words, est 25.8 min (1550.6 s) at 140 wpm, 0 errors, 70 warnings (on-screen reading time). Within the brief's 22-26 min range, so runtime is not critical, but 25.8 is close to the ceiling: every clarity addition below needs a matching cut.
critical: ch02-s06 L0212 'Yet eighty-three years later, someone wrote a network's weights by hand again.' The word 'again', after a jump from 1943 straight to 2026, tells the viewer nobody did it in between. The bible confirms Tracr (DeepMind, 2023, compiles RASP programs into transformer weights) [FR17], Giannou et al. 2023 (a looped transformer programmed as a computer) [FR18] and Percepta (March 2026, a softmax-ReGLU transformer with analytically computed weights) [FR19]. A Hacker News commenter even posted 'google/tracr' in the thread the film covers in ch10 [PJ27]. Experts will catch this at once. Fix: add one line before L0212, e.g. 'Others compile programs into networks too, as proofs and as test beds.' with a text card 'Tracr 2023 · Giannou et al. 2023 · Percepta 2026 · context, not cited by the repo' (claims FR17-FR19, FR22), and change 'again' to 'for an interface'. Cut a word or two elsewhere in ch02 to pay for it.

issues.problem: 'Thirty-two-bit floats' are named but never explained. The whole of Deep Dive I depends on the viewer knowing that a float keeps only about seven significant digits and rounds the rest: the 2^24 edge, the boolean atom's snap, the 1,732-pixel column and the FP32-vs-doubles study. The 15-year-old meets 'rounds to thirty-two-bit floats' as a phrase with no picture behind it.
issues.fix: After L0310 add one sentence for the ear: 'A thirty-two-bit float keeps about seven digits; everything past that is rounded away, at every step.' Show 'FP32: ~7 significant digits' on the plate. Then at L0425 define the other side once: 'JavaScript's usual numbers, sixty-four-bit doubles'.

issues.problem: This is literal code, but on screen it reads as the identity function and contradicts the narration's 'a weighted sum'. Viewers of any level will be puzzled: the affine's 'left' is itself the weighted sum.
issues.fix: Show the evaluated form from PR03 instead: 'affine: value = f(bias) + Σ f(f(weight) × wire), rounded term by term'. If the literal line must stay, add a subscript: 'left = a weighted sum of wires'.

issues.problem: 'Layer' and 'matmul' are never defined in narration (the definition sits on screen only, as a quote). The chapter's key idea is also not explained for the ear: why sums merge (a sum of weighted sums is still one weighted sum, so it is one matrix) and why they stop at a gate (a ReLU bends the line). At 141 words this is the film's thinnest chapter, yet the brief requires 'compilation into one big matmul (fusion, sparsity)'.
issues.fix: L0501: '...a hundred and thirty thin frames. A frame, or layer, holds every step that waits on nothing in it.' L0503: 'The README calls it "a giant matmul": a matrix multiplication, the sum that graphics cards do in bulk. Sums of sums are still sums, so they fold together; a gate bends the line, so nothing merges across one.' Move the '71 of 130 layers' fact into narration ('Seventy-one of those frames are gates, one after another') so the GPU result in s06 has a cause.

issues.where: ch05-s02 L0503 'The sheets of sums fuse'
issues.problem: This overstates the code. CM05 checked the README's GPU claim against the code: sparsity is real (CSR layers), but fusion is partial and layer scheduling is parked (recomputeDepths is off by default). The brief asks the film to state limits honestly.
issues.fix: Say 'fuse where they can' and add a small label: 'sparsity: built · fusion: partial · scheduling: parked (lab/status.md)' (CM05).

issues.problem: 'The familiar order' is never said aloud, so both the teen and the expert have to guess what is being compared. 'The frame you see is a rehearsal, then thrown away' is the film's most important idea about time (HL10, HL14), but here it comes with no setup.
issues.fix: L0613: 'Most interfaces take the input, lay out the page, then advance the animation by however long the frame took. Replay one session at ten frames a second and at a hundred and twenty: that order drifts apart by up to three hundred and fifty-nine pixels.' L0614: '...Only events and settle checks are kept. The frame you see is a preview, worked out from the last kept state and then thrown away.' (HL18, HL10, HL14)

issues.problem: The tree is shown but the narration never says why you would want one: a running total done in a row is a chain where each sum waits for the last (seven steps deep for eight items), while a tree takes three or four levels, and levels are layers. The two prefix-network names are never spoken either; 'these two old names' points at text the viewer may not have read.
issues.fix: L0617: 'A tree. In a row, each total waits for the one before: seven steps deep. Joined in pairs, then pairs of pairs: three or four.' L0618: 'Two old designs do it, Sklansky's and Brent and Kung's, and their names are signed into the runtime itself.' (PT15, PT05)

issues.problem: 'Thirty thousand operations, or one index read' gives the cost but not the mechanism. The brief lists 'one-hot selectors' as a teaching machine, and the arithmetic version is exactly that (PR17: a ReLU one-hot masked sum). Without the mechanism the number is just a number.
issues.fix: Add: 'As arithmetic, you test every row, multiply all but one by nought, and add them up. So the runtime got a fourth instruction: just read the row.' (PR17, PJ23)

issues.problem: 'Slope', 'gradient', 'backwards' and 'backpropagation' arrive one after another, and none is defined. A 15-year-old will not know that a slope here means 'how much the output moves if you nudge this number', or why that is useful for learning.
issues.fix: Before L0705: 'Training asks one question of every number: nudge it, and how far does the output move? That's its slope, or gradient.' Then 'Backwards, the slope for w is nought point four five...'. This also sets up L0712 ('which way to nudge the input').

issues.problem: The gallery's task is never stated, so 'Each edge pulls toward the sketch' refers to a sketch that was never introduced. The viewer does not know what is being learned (where each photo's four edges go) or what it is being compared against (a layout of rectangles, the sketch).
issues.fix: L0714: '...the learned gallery. You sketch a layout of rectangles; it must learn to place the photos on them. Its weights start random, so the photos start in a pile.' (DG04, DG06, DG07)

issues.problem: 'The lab tried that on five numbers' sets up a result and never gives it. The 63.6% and the 24.6% zero-gradient findings (DG20) are the only real unfreezing evidence in the repo, and they sit on a crowded label.
issues.fix: 'The lab tried that on five design numbers: one gradient step solved about two drag frames in three. In one in four, every slope was zero.' (DG20). Pay for it by cutting the label.

issues.problem: 'Multiply every loss by a million, which should change nothing' assumes the viewer knows what a loss is and why scaling it should not matter. The experiment itself (a learned interpreter for two additions) is never named, so '0 out of 20' has no subject.
issues.fix: 'One experiment tried to learn a tiny program, two additions, and scored nought out of twenty. The loss is the number training pushes down; scaling it should change nothing. Multiply it by a million: twenty out of twenty. A tiny constant inside the optimizer had been drowning the signal.' (LB04, LB05)

issues.problem: 'Them' points back to the July briefs' 'established conclusions'. LB03 says the reassessment retired ten earlier claims, not necessarily ten items from that list.
issues.fix: '...a review by an AI agent retired ten earlier claims, the briefs' among them.' (LB03, LB02)

issues.problem: 'A finite machine' is not explained. 'Anything unbounded, like time, has to come from outside' reads as Kleene's claim, but FR07 supports only finite automata and regular events; the 'from outside' line is the film's inference.

issues.where: ch02-s04 L0208 'Calling that a refutation came later.'
issues.problem: This is cryptic for the ear: a refutation of what, and called so by whom? It is also the only 'who doubted and for how long' beat for the oldest tag. The 2020 dendrite finding (FR12), the strongest dated evidence that the tag frayed, is on screen only.

issues.problem: 'At seventeen hundred and thirty-two pixels, doubles count seven columns' is impossible to follow by ear: it never says what is being counted or how.
issues.fix: 'Take a window seventeen hundred and thirty-two pixels wide, with columns two hundred and forty-four wide. JavaScript's doubles count exactly seven. Thirty-two-bit floats round the reciprocal first and land a hair under seven, so "at least seven columns" says no.' (EX03)

strengths: Deep Dive I is genuinely excellent, and correct to the bit: max(0,a−4) − max(0,a−5) gives the clamp; 4.5 gives 11; 4.25 gives 11.5; at a = 16,777,222, a−5 rounds to 2^24, so the bit reads 2 and the answer is 8; the grid-1 compare (relu(5−a), relu(1−ramp)) is 2 ops; the 16-op, 2^149 sign cascade; 8,388,609 = 2^23+1, with ties to even sending 0.5 to 1. I checked each by hand against the bible (TE02-TE08, PR08, PR12, EX05).

'Both belts run' plus 0 × ∞ = NaN is the clearest possible demonstration of why both branches always compute, and the dimmer-switch line ('The program's whole job is to keep it fully on, or fully off') gives both audiences the right mental model.

Deep Dive II's patterns are all worked with real, checkable numbers: findIndex as a count (bits 1 1 1 0 0 → 3), prefix 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 → 3 4 8 9 14 23 25 31, ranks 2 0 3 1 with ties broken by index, filter/slice into 3 slots, the 2×2 spring matrix and its worked step to 401.392 px. The Kleene payoff in ch06-s12 ('The host turns the crank') is earned.

The ReGLU valve's worked gradient (0.225 output, slopes 0.45 and 1.5, then everything going dark at b = −0.4) is correct and makes the dead-gate problem concrete. 'The network learns where. JavaScript decides who.' is a model line for both audiences.

The suspect-tag device works: three wrong guesses die on evidence (ch03-s03, ch03-s06, ch05-s03), and each lab belief gets who/doubted-by/how-long (the July briefs to 3 September, about eight weeks; GPU-is-faster, hours; the TOML rule fixed beforehand). Limits are stated honestly throughout (the validator only in tests, CPU-only runtime, nanoGPT never attempted, the bison drawer still open).

Even-handedness is careful: the contested GPU-vs-RegExp result is shown both ways, the unnamed July conversation is not pinned on Cheng, the AI-agent authorship and the film's own Claude provenance are disclosed, and the Hacker News critic is credited with being right.

The structure pays off: the 4.5 → 11 cold open returns three times (deep dive, the HN stranger, the hidden landing-page comment), and the ending's 'loom of tags' re-uses the compiler's own layering rule as a closing image.
